Metabolic Diseases of the Central Nervous System

Disease Index
🧠

Central Pontine Myelinolysis

LO 1, 2 & 6 Osmotic Demyelination Syndrome
How boards would word it

"A 46-year-old man with a history of alcohol use disorder is admitted with confusion. His initial serum sodium is 101 mEq/L. Over the next 24 hours, his sodium is corrected to 124 mEq/L with hypertonic saline. His mental status initially improves, but 3 days later he develops dysarthria, dysphagia, and progressive quadriparesis. He is afebrile, and cerebrospinal fluid analysis is unremarkable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Central pontine myelinolysis (osmotic demyelination syndrome)
What to look for: the biphasic course — initial improvement of the hyponatremic encephalopathy followed by a delayed second decline days later — plus the setup (severe hyponatremia corrected quickly) and the pontine pattern of spastic quadriparesis with pseudobulbar signs. A normal CSF is doing work here too: it argues against an infectious/inflammatory process like meningoencephalitis, which is the classic distractor for a subacute neurologic decline in a hospitalized patient.
▶
▶ Central pontine myelinolysis
Video — "Central pontine myelinolysis" (YouTube / Osmosis)
1 Natural History
Etiology & Epidemiology

Most commonly caused by overly rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, which puts osmotic stress on brain cells — hyponatremia is the predisposing factor in roughly 78% of cases. CPM can also occur in normo- or hypernatremic patients with other systemic risk factors (~169 published non-hyponatremic cases).

Rare overall (a 14-year Swedish national registry found only 111 patients). Strongly overrepresented in chronic alcoholics (≈70% of registry cases had alcohol use disorder), liver transplant recipients (present in 29% of postmortem exams), malnourished patients, and those with chronic debilitating illness.

Pathophysiology

During chronic hyponatremia, glial cells adapt by extruding organic osmolytes (myoinositol, taurine, glutamate) to avoid cerebral edema. If serum sodium is corrected too fast, extracellular osmolarity rises faster than cells can reaccumulate those osmolytes:

Rapid ↑ in serum Na⁺
→
Osmolyte-depleted glia can't rehydrate
→
Astrocyte injury + BBB disruption
→
Oligodendrocyte apoptosis
→
Demyelination (central pons ± extrapontine)

Pathology shows a symmetric area of myelin destruction in the central basis pontis with preserved neurons/axons and no inflammatory infiltrate — a key point that distinguishes it from an infectious/inflammatory process. Similar symmetric lesions can occur extrapontine (basal ganglia, thalamus, cerebellum, cortical gray-white junctions).

Direction of osmotic shift determines the lesion — rapid correction of hyponatremia (or acute severe hypernatremia) pulls water OUT of brain cells → osmotic demyelination; the reverse (rapid correction of hypernatremia, or acute severe hyponatremia) pushes water IN → cerebral edema and herniation risk.

Prognosis if untreated/unrecognized: historically considered universally fatal when first described at autopsy. With modern MRI diagnosis the picture is broader — a systematic review of 541 patients found 51.9% favorable recovery, 24.8% death, and a combined death-or-permanent-dependence rate of 33–55%. Liver transplant recipients fare far worse (77.4% combined death/disability vs. 44.7% in non-transplant patients).

2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Classic biphasic course

Phase 1 — the underlying hyponatremic encephalopathy initially improves with correction.

Phase 2 — myelinolysis symptoms emerge 1–7 days later; MRI changes can lag another 2–4 weeks behind symptom onset, so an early MRI can look deceptively normal.

Pontine pattern (~50%)

  • Spastic quadriparesis, hyperreflexia (UMN signs)
  • Pseudobulbar palsy — dysarthria, dysphagia
  • Impaired consciousness → coma
  • Locked-in syndrome in severe cases

Extrapontine pattern (~50%, ± pontine)

  • Ataxia (cerebellum — most common extrapontine site)
  • Parkinsonism, dystonia, chorea (basal ganglia)
  • Behavioral changes
Axial fat-saturated T2 MRI — hyperintense signal in the central pons. This patient (alcoholic, admitted with Na⁺ 101, treated with hypertonic saline) developed severe quadriparesis and dysarthria on this timeline.
Axial (outlined) and sagittal MRI — the classic "trident-shaped" T2 hyperintensity in the central pons, with relative sparing of the corticospinal tracts.
Imaging pearl

MRI is the diagnostic modality of choice. Restricted diffusion (DWI) is the earliest and most sensitive acute finding — T2 hyperintensity can be delayed for weeks, so a normal early T2 does not rule this out if the clinical picture fits. Notably, the extent of MRI signal change does not predict clinical outcome.

6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention is the mainstay of management

No evidence-based treatment exists once ODS is established — getting the correction rate right on the front end is everything.

  • Correct chronic hyponatremia by no more than 10–12 mEq/L per 24 hours
  • In high-risk patients (severe hyponatremia ≤105 mmol/L, alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, hypokalemia) — limit correction to ≤8 mEq/L per 24 hours
  • Monitor serum sodium frequently during correction (every 4–6 hours)
  • If overcorrection is caught early, consider re-lowering sodium with desmopressin (DDAVP) and/or hypotonic fluids
  • Identify and correct comorbid electrolyte problems (e.g., hypokalemia) alongside sodium
  • Remember ODS can occur without hyponatremia in at-risk patients — alcohol use disorder, liver disease, and malnutrition are the leading associated risk factors in non-hyponatremic cases too
Pearl

Azotemia (elevated BUN) appears to be somewhat protective against osmotic demyelination in both animal and clinical data — a nice example of how a "bad" lab value can occasionally correlate with a better neurologic outcome in this specific context.

Ethanol Toxicity

LO 1–6
How boards would word it

"A 34-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being found unresponsive outside a bar. He appears malnourished, and his breath smells strongly of alcohol. He has slurred speech, horizontal nystagmus, and an unsteady gait. Vital signs are BP 100/60 mmHg, HR 102/min, RR 10/min. Fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?"

Answer: Administer thiamine before (or together with) IV dextrose
What to look for: a hypoglycemic, likely-malnourished patient with signs of chronic alcohol use is a setup for the "glucose-before-thiamine" trap — giving dextrose alone can precipitate or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy in a thiamine-depleted patient. The nystagmus/ataxia/confusion triad here is also doing double duty as a distractor toward Wernicke-Korsakoff itself, but the vignette is really testing the treatment-sequencing pearl.
1 Natural History
Epidemiology

Alcohol use is extremely common: roughly 85% of adults have used alcohol, and about 10% drink to the point of intoxication. Alcohol is on board in an estimated 15–40% of ED patients. It contributes to about 178,000 deaths per year in the US (~2.6 million globally) — roughly one-third from acute consumption (binge drinking, related accidents) and two-thirds from diseases related to chronic use.

Etiology

Toxicity results from consuming alcohol faster than the liver can metabolize it, producing both direct CNS depressant effects and metabolic derangements from acetaldehyde accumulation.

Pathogenesis
Ethanol
→
↑ GABA-A transmission + ↓ excitatory (glutamate) transmission
→
CNS depression (acute intoxication)
Chronic use
→
Down-regulation of GABA receptors
→
Abrupt cessation unmasks low GABA tone
→
Withdrawal hyperexcitability (anxiety, seizures)

Ethanol also stimulates dopamine release in the mesolimbic reward pathway, reinforcing substance-seeking behavior over time.

Direct pathologic effects

  • Cerebellar (vermal) atrophy
  • Loss of Purkinje and granule cells with Bergmann gliosis
  • Clinically → truncal ataxia
  • Reversible early on; chronic abuse can make changes irreversible

Indirect effects (downstream complications)

  • Vitamin deficiency → Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome or Subacute Combined Degeneration
  • Traumatic CNS injury (falls, accidents)
  • Liver cirrhosis → hyperammonemia → Hepatic Encephalopathy
2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Acute intoxication (typically >5 standard drinks)
  • Slurred speech
  • Nystagmus
  • Disinhibited behavior
  • Loss of coordination, unsteady gait
  • Memory impairment
  • Stupor or coma in severe cases

Associated metabolic derangements

  • Hypoglycemia
  • Lactic acidosis
  • Hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, hypocalcemia, hypophosphatemia
Don't miss a co-ingestion

Traumatic injury is common in intoxicated patients and can be masked by the intoxication itself — a depressed mental status "explained" by a known alcohol level still needs a look for trauma, hypoglycemia, and other co-ingestants before it's written off.

3 Diagnostic Workup
History / physical examLabs / studies
Quantity/timing of intake, last drink, witnessed trauma, co-ingestantsSerum ethanol level — confirmatory
Nystagmus, ataxia, slurred speech, alcohol odor on breathFingerstick glucose (hypoglycemia risk)
Mental status / GCS, signs of traumaBMP — electrolytes, anion gap
Signs of chronic use (malnutrition, stigmata of liver disease)Serum osmolality + osmolar gap (ethanol itself raises the gap — account for its contribution before attributing an elevated gap to another toxic alcohol)
—LFTs, lactate, ABG; CT head if trauma or if mental status doesn't track with the ethanol level
Differential: the other toxic alcohols

Methanol, ethylene glycol, and isopropyl alcohol are separate "toxic alcohols" that can mimic ethanol intoxication but carry different antidotes and complications — a frequent board differential:

AgentDistinguishing clueAGMA?Antidote
EthanolClassic intoxication pattern above; contributes to (not just mimics) the osmolar gapNo (mild lactic acidosis at most)None — supportive
MethanolVisual disturbance/blindness, papilledemaYes (formic acid)Fomepizole ± hemodialysis
Ethylene glycolFlank pain, hematuria, oxalate crystalluria, urine fluoresces under Wood's lampYes (glycolic acid)Fomepizole ± hemodialysis; adjunct thiamine/pyridoxine
Isopropyl alcoholFruity breath, ketosis without acidosisNoNone — avoid fomepizole (prolongs its effect)
4 Treatment
Approach

Supportive care

  • ABCs — airway protection if stuporous/comatose
  • IV fluids
  • Correct hypoglycemia with dextrose — but give thiamine first or alongside in malnourished/chronic-use patients to avoid precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Repleate electrolytes (K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, phosphate)

Agitation / withdrawal

  • Benzodiazepines for agitation or withdrawal seizures
  • CIWA-Ar protocol to guide dosing
Methanol & ethylene glycol metabolism — alcohol dehydrogenase converts each to its toxic metabolite; fomepizole (or ethanol itself) works by competitively inhibiting alcohol dehydrogenase, the same enzyme that starts ethanol's own metabolism. Thiamine and pyridoxine are cofactors that shunt ethylene glycol's glycolic acid away from oxalic acid — part of why thiamine repletion matters broadly in alcohol-use patients, not just for Wernicke prevention.
Mnemonic

FOMEpizole — For Overdosing on Methanol or Ethylene glycol. Fomepizole is not indicated for isolated ethanol or isopropyl alcohol toxicity.

5 Monitoring & Long-Term Complications
Monitoring
  • Serial CIWA-Ar scoring for withdrawal, which typically peaks 24–72 hours after the last drink
  • Trend electrolytes and glucose during repletion
  • Trend LFTs in patients with chronic use
Long-term complications of chronic use
  • Cerebellar (vermal) atrophy → persistent truncal ataxia
  • Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome (thiamine deficiency)
  • Subacute Combined Degeneration (B12 deficiency)
  • Hepatic Encephalopathy (cirrhosis → hyperammonemia)
  • Recurrent traumatic brain injury
6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Screening & prevention
  • Screen with validated tools (AUDIT-C, CAGE) at routine visits and ED encounters
  • Brief intervention / SBIRT counseling for at-risk drinking
  • Referral to addiction treatment / counseling for alcohol use disorder
  • Prophylactic thiamine repletion in chronic heavy drinkers, especially before glucose administration, to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy
  • Counsel on safe-drinking limits and the risks of rapid/binge consumption

Hepatic Encephalopathy

LO 1–2 Portosystemic Encephalopathy
How boards would word it

"A 58-year-old man with a history of alcoholic cirrhosis is brought in by his family for 3 days of worsening confusion. He has not had a bowel movement in 5 days. On exam he is disoriented, and when asked to hold his arms outstretched with wrists extended, he demonstrates intermittent, non-rhythmic flapping movements of the hands. He denies GI bleeding, and vital signs are stable. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Hepatic encephalopathy, precipitated by constipation
What to look for: known cirrhosis plus a subacute confusional state is the setup; the described hand-flapping is asterixis, not a true tremor (it's an intermittent lapse in postural tone, not a rhythmic oscillation) — boards will often describe it exactly this way instead of naming it, to make sure the exam finding itself is recognized. The 5 days of constipation is the precipitant being tested: reduced gut transit time means more time for colonic bacteria to generate and for the gut to absorb ammonia. Denying GI bleeding is there to let you rule out the other classic precipitant.
▶
▶ Hepatic Encephalopathy — Pathophysiology, Stages and West Haven Criteria
Video — "Hepatic Encephalopathy: Pathophysiology, Stages and West Haven Criteria" (YouTube / AMBOSS)
1 Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology

Caused by underlying liver dysfunction (cirrhosis — e.g., from chronic alcohol use or Wilson disease — or acute liver failure) with portosystemic shunting of blood around the liver. 30–40% of cirrhotic patients will experience an episode of overt hepatic encephalopathy at some point in their course, while subtler (covert) signs are detectable in up to ~70% of cirrhotics if specifically tested for.

↑ Ammonia absorption/production

  • Infection (e.g., spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, SIRS)
  • GI bleeding
  • Constipation
  • ↑ dietary protein intake
  • Hypokalemia

↓ Ammonia metabolism/clearance

  • Renal failure
  • Portal vein thrombosis
  • Portosystemic shunts (e.g., after TIPS)
  • Hypovolemia (dehydration, diarrhea, vomiting)
  • Metabolic alkalosis; diuretic use
Pathophysiology — the ammonia theory (leading mechanism)
Cirrhosis
→
↓ hepatic metabolism + portosystemic shunting
→
↑ blood ammonia (NH3)
→
crosses BBB, taken up by astrocytes
→
converted to glutamine
→
↑ osmotic pressure → cellular swelling
→
cerebral edema, ↑ICP, neuro deterioration

Normally the liver clears ~90% of ammonia; in HE this fails, and the astrocytes doing the brain's ammonia clean-up become the injury itself — high NH3 damages the very astrocytes responsible for removing it, creating a self-reinforcing cycle. Pathologic specimens show abnormal (Type II) astrocytes in the cerebral cortex.

Two electrolyte/acid-base effects worth knowing: hypokalemia drives a compensatory K⁺-out/H⁺-in shift → intracellular acidosis → stimulates renal tubular cells to generate more ammonia. Metabolic alkalosis reduces available H⁺, shifting the NH3/NH4⁺ equilibrium toward more NH3 (the form that crosses the BBB freely) — both worsen encephalopathy independent of any change in total ammonia production.

GABA-benzodiazepine theory

↑ endogenous GABA and benzodiazepine-like substances are produced in the brain and escape clearance by the failing liver, accumulating and producing cognitive impairment.

Unity theory

Hyperammonemia itself inhibits GABA metabolism, prolonging its action as an inhibitory neurotransmitter — linking the ammonia and GABA mechanisms into one pathway rather than two competing explanations.

Classification

By cause: Type A (acute liver failure), B (portosystemic bypass), C (cirrhosis). By severity: covert (abnormal only on psychometric/neurophysiologic testing) vs. overt (West Haven grade ≥II). By course: episodic, recurrent, or persistent; precipitated or nonprecipitated.

Prognosis: symptoms are usually reversible with correction of the precipitant. However, the precipitants themselves — especially infection and GI bleeding — carry substantial mortality independent of the encephalopathy, and recurrent/persistent HE reflects advancing liver disease.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Spectrum — mild to severe
Fatigue, apathy, mild confusion
→
Disorientation, irritability, memory loss, ↑ psychomotor activity
→
Drowsiness → stupor → coma

Other reported features: impaired sleep patterns, slurred speech, and socially aberrant behavior (e.g., urinating or defecating in public, shouting at strangers) — a vivid but genuinely testable early clue in an otherwise mild presentation.

Asterixis — the signature exam finding

Asterixis ("a-" + Greek sterixis, "fixed position") is an intermittent lapse in postural control, elicited by asking the patient to extend the wrists/fingers and observing an irregular flapping movement — it is not a true (rhythmic) tremor. It is not specific to HE (also seen in uremia, CO2 narcosis, some drug toxicities), but in the right clinical context it's the single most recognizable bedside finding.

Other neurologic findings as severity progresses

  • Grimacing, primitive suck and grasp reflexes
  • Exaggerated or asymmetric deep tendon reflexes
  • Babinski sign
  • Muscle rigidity
  • Focal or generalized seizures

Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency

LO 1–3 Beriberi
How boards would word it

"A 52-year-old woman presents with progressive leg swelling and shortness of breath 8 months after gastric bypass surgery. She also reports several weeks of numbness and tingling in both feet. Vital signs show a heart rate of 118/min. Exam reveals bilateral lower-extremity edema with warm extremities and bounding peripheral pulses. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Wet beriberi (thiamine / vitamin B1 deficiency)
What to look for: a malabsorptive risk factor (gastric bypass) plus the combination of high-output cardiac failure and peripheral neuropathy is the pattern to catch. Warm extremities and bounding pulses are the key distractor-busters here — they point away from a typical low-output cardiomyopathy (which would have cool, poorly perfused extremities) and toward the systemic vasodilation of wet beriberi.
1 Natural History
Etiology & Risk Factors

Thiamine is a water-soluble vitamin that must be obtained from the diet — the body has minimal reserves, so deficiency develops quickly once intake or absorption falls off. Risk factors include:

  • Heavy/chronic alcohol use (poor intake + impaired absorption/storage)
  • Malnutrition, starvation (including famine-affected regions)
  • Malabsorption, bariatric surgery
  • Prolonged vomiting or diarrhea
  • Diuretics, hemodialysis
  • Malignancy
  • States of increased demand — hyperthyroidism, pregnancy
Pathophysiology
↓ Thiamine
→
impaired oxidative glucose metabolism (pyruvate/α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase cofactor)
→
ATP depletion
→
damage concentrated in highly aerobic tissue (brain, heart)

This is also the mechanistic reason large glucose loads are dangerous in a thiamine-depleted patient: metabolizing that glucose consumes even more of the little remaining thiamine, which can acutely precipitate the CNS component of this disease (Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome — see that tab for the full picture).

Pathology

The CNS lesions of thiamine deficiency are foci of hemorrhage and necrosis in structures surrounding the third ventricle — classically the mammillary bodies, but also the periaqueductal gray/colliculi, thalamus, and hypothalamus. These lesions are later infiltrated by macrophages and can eventually become cystic.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Course

Early: anorexia is often the first, nonspecific sign. Prolonged deficiency produces the full beriberi syndrome below, plus systemic features: worsening macrocytic anemia with jaundice, and glossitis with a painful, tender tongue that has lost its papillae.

The four faces of thiamine deficiency — CNS (Wernicke/Korsakoff) findings above the midline, systemic (dry/wet beriberi) findings below.

Dry beriberi

  • Symmetric sensorimotor peripheral neuropathy
  • Muscle weakness, progressive wasting
  • Paresthesias, numbness
  • Decreased deep tendon reflexes
  • Calf pain
  • Confusion; paralysis in advanced cases

Wet beriberi

  • High-output cardiac failure (from systemic vasodilation)
  • Dilated cardiomyopathy, cardiomegaly
  • Tachycardia, dyspnea
  • Peripheral edema
  • Warm extremities, bounding pulses (vs. cool periphery of typical low-output HF)
CNS component — don't duplicate, cross-reference

In alcohol use disorder especially, thiamine deficiency frequently produces Wernicke encephalopathy (gaze palsies/ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, confusion) and, if unrecognized, Korsakoff syndrome (amnesia and confabulation). The two often occur together. See the Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome tab for the full clinical and treatment picture — this panel focuses on the systemic (beriberi) manifestations.

Infantile beriberi (distinct pediatric variant)

Cardiomegaly, tachycardia, cyanosis, and an aseptic-meningitis-like picture (vomiting, seizures) in breastfed infants of thiamine-deficient mothers.

3 Diagnostic Workup
History / physical examLabs
Risk factors: alcohol use, malnutrition, bariatric surgery, malabsorption, prolonged vomiting/diarrhea, dialysis↑ RBC transketolase activity after thiamine administration — the classic confirmatory test (thiamine is a required cofactor for transketolase, so a brisk rise in activity confirms prior deficiency)
Symmetric peripheral neuropathy, decreased DTRs, calf tendernessDirect serum/whole-blood thiamine level (less commonly available/used)
Signs of high-output heart failure: tachycardia, edema, warm extremities, bounding pulsesCBC — may show macrocytic anemia
Glossitis, tongue tenderness/papillary loss—
Gaze palsy, ataxia, confusion — suggests CNS extension (see Wernicke-Korsakoff tab)—
Pearl

Think "Dry = nerve Damage, Wet = Water" — dry beriberi is a peripheral neuropathy, wet beriberi adds the fluid overload of high-output heart failure. Many patients have overlapping features of both.

Wilson Disease

LO 1–2 Hepatolenticular Degeneration
How boards would word it

"A 19-year-old college student is brought in by his roommate for 6 months of worsening tremor and clumsiness. His roommate also reports he has become unusually irritable and withdrawn. On exam he has a low-frequency tremor that worsens when his arms are outstretched, dysarthria, and mild jaundice. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral golden-brown rings at the corneal periphery. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Wilson disease
What to look for: the combination that clinches it is young age (Wilson has a strong age preference for onset between 5–35) plus simultaneous hepatic (jaundice) and neuropsychiatric (tremor, dysarthria, personality change) findings — that pairing alone should raise Wilson disease before any eye finding is mentioned. The Kayser-Fleischer rings and the "wing-beating" quality of the tremor are the confirmatory details layered on top. A Parkinson-disease distractor is built into the tremor description, which is exactly why the age and the liver findings matter so much here.
1 Natural History
Epidemiology

Onset is typically between 5 and 35 years (mean 12–23 years). US prevalence is roughly 1 in 30,000, though this varies substantially by region — from about 1 in 30,000 in Japan to 1 in 100,000 in Australia — largely tracking with rates of consanguinity, since this is an autosomal recessive condition (heterozygote carrier rate ≈1 in 100).

Pathophysiology
Autosomal recessive ATP7B mutation (chromosome 13)
→
defective copper-transporting ATPase (Wilson protein)
→
↓ copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin AND ↓ biliary copper excretion
→
copper accumulates in hepatocytes → spills into blood (↑ free serum copper)
→
deposition in liver, cornea, CNS (basal ganglia, brainstem, cerebellum), kidneys

The paradox worth remembering: total serum copper and ceruloplasmin are both low (less copper is being loaded onto ceruloplasmin), while free (non-ceruloplasmin-bound) serum copper is high — it's this unbound fraction that deposits in tissue and does the damage.

Normal (left) vs. Wilson disease (right) hepatocyte copper handling. In Wilson disease, the mutant Wilson protein (ATP7B) blocks copper from reaching the Golgi for ceruloplasmin loading (step 3) and from being excreted into bile (step 4) — copper backs up in the hepatocyte and leaks into plasma as unbound copper (step 6).

Prognosis: untreated Wilson disease is progressive and eventually fatal, from either liver failure or neurologic deterioration. The prognosis is good if the diagnosis is made and treatment started early — which is exactly why recognizing the pattern (young patient + liver disease + neuropsychiatric findings) matters so much.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation

Hepatic

  • Hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice, ascites, abdominal pain
  • Acute or chronic hepatitis (can mimic autoimmune hepatitis)
  • Cirrhosis, portal hypertension
  • Hepatic encephalopathy
  • Can present as acute liver failure

Ocular

  • Kayser-Fleischer rings — copper in Descemet membrane → 1–2mm golden/green-brown peripheral corneal rings. Characteristic, but absence does not rule out the diagnosis
  • Sunflower cataracts — copper deposits in the lens

Neurologic & psychiatric

  • Cerebellar: dysarthria (most common), gait abnormalities, choreoathetosis
  • Extrapyramidal: dystonia, parkinsonism
  • Tremor — often asymmetric; may include a "wing-beating" tremor (low-frequency, high-amplitude, most prominent with arms outstretched)
  • Drooling (oropharyngeal dysphagia), seizures, cognitive impairment
  • Depression, irritability, psychosis — can precede other findings
Wilson disease findings mapped by system — Kayser-Fleischer rings (eyes), copper deposits in the basal ganglia with drooling/dysarthria/dystonia/rigidity/asymmetric tremor (brain), and hepatitis/cirrhosis/jaundice (liver).
Pearl

Suspect Wilson disease whenever otherwise-unexplained liver disease and a movement disorder or psychiatric change show up in the same young patient — that pairing, more than any single finding, is what should trigger the workup.

Subacute Combined Degeneration

LO 1–2 Dorsal Columns + Lateral Corticospinal Tract B12 (Cobalamin) Deficiency
How boards would word it

"A 67-year-old man presents with several months of progressive numbness and tingling in his feet, followed more recently by unsteady gait and leg stiffness. He reports fatigue and a strict vegan diet for the past 15 years. On exam he has loss of vibration and proprioception in both feet, hyperreflexia at the knees, bilateral Babinski signs, and a positive Romberg test. He also appears mildly pale with a smooth, red tongue. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"

Answer: Subacute combined degeneration (vitamin B12 deficiency)
What to look for: the combination of dorsal column loss (vibration/proprioception, positive Romberg) plus corticospinal tract signs (hyperreflexia, Babinski) is the "combined" pattern that names this disease — sensory ataxia and upper motor neuron signs together in the same patient. The dietary history (long-standing vegan diet) and the systemic clues (pallor, glossitis) point straight to B12 deficiency as the cause rather than a primary neurologic disease.
1 Natural History
Definition, Epidemiology & Etiology

A disease of the large myelinated sensory and motor systems of the peripheral nerves, spinal cord, and brain — degeneration occurs in the peripheral nerves and in the posterior and lateral columns of the spinal cord, secondary to vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency. Synonyms: SCD, vitamin B12 deficiency, posterolateral sclerosis.

  • Predominantly affects adults >40, with highest incidence age 50–80
  • B12 deficiency is the most common cause, but not all B12-deficient individuals develop SCD — B12 deficiency affects 5–12% of the elderly population, and SCD develops in only about 14% of those with confirmed deficiency

Causes of the underlying B12 deficiency:

  • Malabsorption — failure to transfer B12 across the intestinal wall
  • Pernicious anemia — autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor — is a classic associated cause
  • Nitrous oxide exposure (recreational or anesthetic) inactivates B12 and can precipitate SCD
  • Vegan diets are low in B12; risk is greater in young children, pregnant women, and the elderly
  • Other risk factors: gastric abnormalities, small bowel disease, pancreatic disease, raw freshwater fish consumption, genetic abnormalities
Pathophysiology
B12 deficiency
→
impaired myelin fatty-acid synthesis
→
spongy vacuolation + intramyelinic/interstitial edema
→
myelin destruction + astrocytosis

B12 is required for the fatty-acid synthesis pathway that produces and maintains myelin. Degeneration initially targets the heavily myelinated posterior and lateral columns; over time, both ascending sensory and descending motor tracts become demyelinated, affecting the dorsal column, spinocerebellar, and corticospinal systems of the spinal cord.

Myelin stain (black = intact myelin) — thoracic (A) and lumbar (B) spinal cord sections; pale areas in the dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tract indicate demyelination.

Prognosis: this is one of the few myelopathies that is genuinely treatable — signs and symptoms can be reversible if B12 deficiency is corrected early. Once complete paraplegia has developed, however, recovery is poor, which is exactly why early recognition matters so much here.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Presentation

Subacute, progressive, diffuse and symmetric: begins bilaterally with posterior column signs (paresthesias, reduced touch/joint/pressure sensation), followed over several weeks by spastic weakness and eventually ataxic paraplegia.

  • Insidious onset, often first noticed as paresthesias in the hands and feet
  • Loss of proprioception and vibratory sense; spasticity and ataxic weakness usually limited to the legs
  • Visual impairment from optic neuropathy (optic atrophy)
  • Frontal white matter cognitive symptoms — signs of (reversible) dementia, depression, or paranoia
  • Autonomic dysfunction: impotence, incontinence
Systemic clues (pernicious anemia)

Depending on etiology, signs and symptoms of pernicious anemia may accompany the neurologic picture: fatigue, pallor, mild scleral icterus/jaundice, and glossitis.

Pearl

The "combined" in subacute combined degeneration refers to simultaneous dorsal column and lateral corticospinal tract involvement — sensory ataxia and vibration/proprioception loss plus spasticity, hyperreflexia, and a Babinski sign together in the same patient. (Note: coexisting peripheral neuropathy can sometimes blunt the expected hyperreflexia, so the exam picture can look mixed.)

Mimic to remember

Copper deficiency can mimic SCD almost exactly — worth checking if B12 comes back normal but the clinical picture otherwise fits.

🧠 Practice Questions — Subacute Combined Degeneration

Wernicke-Korsakoff Syndrome

LO 1–6 Thiamine (Vitamin B1) Deficiency
How boards would word it

"A 54-year-old man with chronic alcohol use disorder is brought to the emergency department for acute confusion. On exam he has horizontal nystagmus and a wide-based, unsteady gait. He is afebrile with a nonfocal neurologic exam otherwise. His family says he has eaten very little in the past two weeks. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate next step?"

Answer: Immediate IV thiamine (before any glucose administration)
What to look for: the classic triad — confusion, oculomotor dysfunction (nystagmus here), and gait ataxia — in a patient with an alcohol-use and malnutrition history is Wernicke encephalopathy until proven otherwise. This is a medical emergency: treatment (IV thiamine) should never wait for labs or imaging, and thiamine must be given before any dextrose to avoid precipitating or worsening the encephalopathy.

▶ Wernicke Korsakoff Syndrome (Year of the Zebra)
Video — "Wernicke Korsakoff Syndrome" (YouTube / Year of the Zebra)
Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome at a glance — Wernicke encephalopathy (acute, reversible) on the left of the comparison, Korsakoff syndrome (chronic, irreversible) on the right, with shared etiology/pathophysiology/diagnosis/treatment summarized in the panel at far left.
1 Natural History
Epidemiology & Etiology

Both conditions result from severe deficiency of thiamine (vitamin B1). Chronic heavy alcohol use is the most common cause — occurring in roughly 3% of the US alcoholic population — due to inadequate intake, impaired absorption, and reduced hepatic storage of thiamine. Nonalcohol-related cases account for an estimated 20–25% of cases identified at autopsy.

Other causes of thiamine deficiency

  • Inadequate intake — thiamine-deficient diets, anorexia nervosa, starvation
  • Malabsorption; GI disease
  • Increased demand — pregnancy/lactation (hyperemesis), hyperthyroidism, systemic illness, malignancy
  • Increased loss — diarrhea, dialysis
  • Prolonged IV feeding without proper supplementation

Also reported with

  • Transplantation, hemodialysis, or peritoneal dialysis
  • AIDS
  • Extreme/restrictive diets
Pathophysiology
Thiamine deficiency
→
↓ thiamine pyrophosphate (cofactor for cerebral glucose/energy metabolism)
→
↓ ATP + ↑ free radicals
→
injury to myelin, BBB, neurotransmitter systems
→
impaired axonal conduction → Wernicke symptoms

In Korsakoff syndrome, long-term thiamine deficiency causes permanent damage to limbic structures — especially the mammillary bodies and anterior thalamic nuclei — producing atrophy and the resulting memory loss, apathy, and disrupted emotional processing.

Lesion distribution: paraventricular regions of the third ventricle and cerebral aqueduct — thalamus, hypothalamus, midbrain. Early lesions show vascular congestion, microglial proliferation, and petechial hemorrhages; later findings include demyelination, gliosis, and loss of neuropil, with atrophy of the mammillary bodies and loss of Purkinje cells in the anterior cerebellum.

Coronal gross specimen — the mammillary bodies (white arrows), part of the limbic system, are a characteristic site of necrosis and atrophy in Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

Prognosis: Wernicke encephalopathy is acute and reversible with prompt treatment — oculomotor findings typically resolve within hours, ataxia within days, and confusion within weeks. Korsakoff syndrome, in contrast, is chronic and its deficits are usually irreversible.

2 Typical Clinical Presentation
Wernicke encephalopathy — classic triad

Should be suspected in any patient with chronic heavy alcohol use who presents with one or more of:

  • Confusion (the most common of the three)
  • Oculomotor dysfunction — gaze-induced horizontal/vertical nystagmus (most common), diplopia, conjugate gaze palsy
  • Gait ataxia — wide-based, small steps

The full triad is present in only a minority of patients — estimates range from about 10% up to a third — so any single element in the right clinical context should raise suspicion.

Other Wernicke manifestations

  • Autonomic dysfunction — hypotension, syncope, hypothermia
  • Peripheral neuropathy — paresthesia, foot drop, ↓ DTRs
  • Cardiovascular — tachycardia, exertional dyspnea
  • Diencephalic involvement — stupor, coma

Korsakoff syndrome (chronic, irreversible)

  • Confabulation — fabricated memories filling in gaps
  • Anterograde and retrograde amnesia (anterograde more common)
  • Personality changes (frontal lobe) — apathy, indifference, ↓ executive function
  • Disorientation to time, place, and person
  • Hallucinations
Mnemonics

Wernicke's COAT: Confusion, Oculomotor dysfunction, Ataxia, and Thiamine administration.
Korsakoff's CART: Confabulation, Anterograde and Retrograde amnesia, altered Temper.

Axial T2-weighted MRI — bilateral, symmetric hyperintensities characteristic of Wernicke encephalopathy.
3 Diagnostic Workup
History / physical examLabs / imaging
Alcohol use history, dietary history, GI surgery, hyperemesis/pregnancy↓ Serum thiamine; ↓ erythrocyte transketolase activity (thiamine-dependent enzyme)
Assess for the classic triad; vestibular testing (often impaired)↑ Serum lactate and pyruvate
CAGE screen for alcohol use disorderEvidence of alcohol-related liver dysfunction
—Brain MRI: T2 hyperintensities in mammillary bodies, midbrain tectal plate, dorsomedial thalamic nuclei, cerebellum, and around the aqueduct/third ventricle; periventricular hemorrhage and/or mammillary body atrophy are frequent in both conditions
Don't wait

This is usually a clinical diagnosis. Laboratory tests and imaging can support an ambiguous case, but they should never delay treatment — give thiamine empirically as soon as Wernicke encephalopathy is suspected.

Wernicke differential (acute delirium/ataxia)

  • Cerebellar stroke
  • Hypoxia/hypercarbia (post-arrest)
  • Postictal state
  • CNS infections (e.g., meningitis)
  • Tabes dorsalis

Korsakoff differential (amnesia/disorientation)

  • Alzheimer disease
  • Dementia with Lewy bodies
  • Parkinson disease
4 Treatment

Wernicke encephalopathy — medical emergency

  • Immediate high-dose IV thiamine until symptoms recede, then a lower maintenance dose
  • Thiamine before IV glucose — glucose without thiamine can worsen encephalopathy
  • Long-term oral vitamin B-complex (B1, B6, B12, folic acid)
  • Alcohol abstinence

Korsakoff syndrome

  • Oral thiamine to prevent further progression
  • Alcohol abstinence
  • Psychiatric/psychological therapy; memory aids (e.g., signs/arrows at home)
  • Acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (e.g., donepezil) may offer some cognitive benefit
The single highest-yield sequencing pearl in this whole note

Thiamine before glucose — always. Every alcohol-use, malnutrition, or hypoglycemia scenario elsewhere in this Disease Index (Ethanol Toxicity, Thiamine Deficiency) points back to this same rule: glucose metabolism consumes thiamine, and giving dextrose to a thiamine-depleted patient can precipitate or worsen the very syndrome described on this page.

5 Monitoring & Complications
What to watch for

Recovery with thiamine repletion can be dramatic in Wernicke encephalopathy — track the expected timeline (oculomotor findings within hours, ataxia within days, confusion within weeks) to confirm response to treatment.

Watch for and manage complications, including:

  • Signs and symptoms of alcohol withdrawal
  • Liver failure
  • Systemic infection
6 Prevention & Health Promotion
Prevention
  • Lifestyle changes; avoidance of alcohol
  • Improved diet / nutritional supplementation, particularly in at-risk populations (chronic heavy alcohol use, malnutrition, hyperemesis, prolonged unsupplemented IV feeding)
  • Prophylactic thiamine repletion before glucose administration in any at-risk patient — the same principle covered under Ethanol Toxicity and Thiamine Deficiency
